Both of the peaked attention outputs have an unusual top direction. Layer 1's o_proj writes a direction concentrated on just 8 channels: channels 23, 163, 537, 369 and 238 at about ±0.37 to 0.45, plus 400, 97 and 639. Channels 163, 400, 97 and 639 are massive-activation channels (residual RMS 94 to 841, against a median of 1.1), but 537, 369 and 238 are ordinary small channels (RMS about 1.1). Layer 12's o_proj top direction is likewise spread over about 8 channels (24, 629, 353, 262, 196, 163, 87, 639). Its four main ones are ordinary-sized there (ranks 282 to 472 of 640). A few ordinary channels at near-equal weights is not what a dense learned feature looks like, but it could be Gemma's normal attention-sink bookkeeping.

Two weight-only checks can tell these apart.
- **Is the sparsity special to L1 and L12?** I'll compute the same statistics (s1/s2, number of channels above 0.05, top channels) for the top output direction of all 18 o_proj matrices. If every layer looks like this, it is an architectural feature.
- **Does the direction come from one value?** Because the four heads share one value head, I'll check whether the top input direction reads the same value-space direction from all four heads. If it does, it is the constant value of whatever token every head attends to, typically the BOS sink.

Sparse top directions everywhere, or a shared value direction, would make this natural sink machinery. A sparse direction only in L1 and L12, read unevenly, would be worth a causal test.

The sparse top directions are not special to layers 1 and 12. Most layers' o_proj have a top output direction concentrated on 2 to 8 channels:
- L3 and L16 put almost everything on one channel;
- L11, L13, L14, L15 and L17 use 4 to 6 channels;
- the head blocks read partly shared value directions (cosines 0.3 to 0.75).

This is the model's normal outlier-channel structure, so the weight-anomaly line is closed.

My earlier contrasts also have a gap. Every math-versus-non-math comparison of neurons and directions used answer tokens (positions 60 to 120). A gating mechanism could detect math in the problem statement instead: an early neuron that fires on the prompt and writes a "mode" signal that later layers pick up through attention. That would evade all of those tests, and the framing tests too, since the problem text is the same in every frame.

Using pass 2's stored MLP activations (128 math prompts with own answers, 48 non-math chats, all 18 layers), I'll compute each neuron's mean activation over prompt tokens per text. I'll then take the standardized math-minus-non-math difference across texts (Cohen's d) and report, per layer, the most selective neurons and the 99th percentile of |d|. A natural model has many moderately selective topic neurons with a smooth tail. A planted gate would show as a lone neuron with a far larger d than everything else, which would then get its weights examined and a causal ablation screen.

Prompt-token selectivity shows no lone gate. Every layer has dozens to hundreds of neurons with |d| > 4 between math prompts and non-math chats, as expected since the prompts differ in topic, length and the instruction. The tails are smooth: the top three in each layer sit close together (for example −10.5, 9.3, 9.1 in L3), and no single neuron stands far above the rest. So nothing looks like an implanted detector, and this check also comes back natural.

One gating hypothesis is still untested and needs a pass. A "math mode" set by a word-problem context could persist and degrade arithmetic even in a later, neutral request. I'll build a paired teacher-forced test in which the same bare arithmetic probe ("Calculate a op b." answered with "a op b = c", equations taken from DEV gold solutions) follows one of three contexts:
- a completed GSM8K exchange,
- a completed non-math chat of similar length,
- nothing.

For a natural model, arithmetic after a math context should be about as good as after a non-math one, or slightly better from priming. Clearly worse arithmetic after the math context would reveal a persistent gate whose direction I could then localize.
